entities.summary:
Jacques-François Lefranc (1739-1792) was a French Jesuit priest and a prominent anti-Masonic author whose writings significantly fueled counter-revolutionary discourse during the tumultuous years of the French Revolution. Born in Vire, Normandy, Lefranc's intellectual and theological formation within the Society of Jesus provided him with a rigorous foundation, which he later applied to his polemical critiques of Enlightenment-era secret societies. His life and tragic death in the September Massacres of 1792 encapsulate the profound ideological clashes and escalating violence that characterized the late 18th century, making him a potent symbol for royalist and Catholic resistance.

Ordained a priest in 1763, Lefranc rose to become the superior of the Eudist seminary at Caen. However, it was his prolific literary output against Freemasonry that cemented his historical footprint. His most influential work, 'Le Voile levé pour les curieux, ou le secret de la Révolution de France révélé à l'aide de la Franc-Maçonnerie' (1791), posited a vast, intricate conspiracy by Freemasons, philosophers, and Protestants to dismantle the French monarchy and the Catholic Church. This text, published amidst revolutionary fervor, articulated a narrative that resonated deeply with those seeking to explain the radical societal upheaval through the lens of clandestine machinations.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Jacques-François Lefranc's anti-Masonic writings significantly shaped counter-revolutionary ideology, influencing later conspiracy theorists like Barruel and providing a framework for explaining the French Revolution. His martyrdom during the September Massacres also made him a potent symbol for royalist and Catholic resistance.
